items.title: llm-gemini 0.36
items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.36

Gemini 4 Carbon was announced two weeks ago for "a subset of cyber defenders", but today it's available to everyone else.

This is Google's best ever Gemini, priced at $2/million input and $10/million output at launch (that's GPT-6.1 Sol / Claude Sonnet 5.5 prices) but scheduled to double in price to $4/$20 on December 1st (same as Opus 5.5).

Here are three pelicans for the low, medium and high thinking efforts (it defaults to medium). This is the pelican I got for high:

Gemini pelicans have all been great for a while now, so I also tested it out using Google's Antigravity IDE with a prompt I first tried with Claude Fable 5.2 yesterday:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the HTML result (I had to prompt "build that into a standalone HTML file" to get a version with no external dependencies). I then screen-captured that as a video:

Update: Huh, just saw this on YouTube:

Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music.

items.title: Google Finds that Technical Debt Can Derail Coding Agents Through "Agent Distraction"
items.summary:
In a recent article, Google senior staff software engineer Sam Saccone and senior staff data scientist Madhuri Garikapati highlighted the cost of agent distraction, where AI coding agents get derailed by stale technical debt, such as old TODO comments, obsolete bug references, and outdated specs, leading them to embark on unrequested "side-quests".

By Sergio De Simone

items.summary: See how Workday used LangGraph and LangSmith to build an internal AI agent platform that cut prototype time from months to less than a day and compliance needs.
items.story_key: model:langgraph|title:how workday built an enterprise scale ai agent platform with langgraph and langs
items.content_excerpt: Workday is the trusted agentic platform for HR, finance, and IT, serving more than half the Fortune 500. The team set out to create the internal developer platform to build, deploy, and run AI agents in production, on Workday's infrastructure. The team leveraged LangGraph for agent orchestration and LangSmith for tracing, observability, and evals. In 2025, Workday’s leadership team saw the market opportunity for building agentic solutions and set an ambitious goal for agents in production by the end of 2026. Product teams needed a platform that could support both rapid prototyping and production deployments—a uniquely challenging mandate given Workday operates under some of the strictest security and data governance requirements in enterprise software. Getting any internal service into production means satisfying demanding audit, compliance, and data retention policies. The surface area was enormous for a team of four, encompassing a durable, scalable agent server; data access controls tied to Workday's audit policies; a collaborative eval platform; and an SDK that abstracted all of it. Workday’s Agent Platform team serves two user bases. 1.) the internal Workday engineering teams building agents, and 2.) the end customers of those agents. It lets teams focus on functional requirements, while handling authentication, security, compliance, and infrastructure. The first major product shipped was Workday's Agent System of Record, a governance layer that controls which APIs the agents are allowed to access. The Agent Platform team built the backend server and eval infrastructure that the system of record runs on top of. The team also built what Alex Gatto, Senior Machine Learning Engineer, describes as "Workday LangChain": a Python SDK that wraps LangChain primitives and routes them through Workday's internal services, including an LLM gateway, a RAG retrieval service, and other internal tooling. "Anytime there was some AI concept that LangChain had put out, we tried to build a Python SDK for that same concept, but at Workday," explained Alex. Workday chose LangGraph for agent orchestration to give internal developers maximum flexibility at the design layer, while providing standardized infrastructure underneath. items.story_key: model:gemini|ver:4|title:gemini 4 carbon is now available
items.content_excerpt: Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively

items.title: Which Claude model should you build with? Fable, Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku
items.summary: Which Claude model to pick, what they cost, and how to use them together.
items.story_key: model:claude|title:which claude model should you build with fable opus sonnet or haiku
items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code, you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in Spending your effort , on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens. On the hardest work, the price gap can close. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high scored about level with Opus 5.5 at max (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. So before you raise Opus 5.5 past high on a hard task, test Fable 5.2. For everyday work, Opus 5.5 at medium is still the place to start. For benchmark results, see the launch post . However,

NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek. Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. items.title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
items.summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
items.story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
items.content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send. Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request

items.title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
items.summary: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.

items.title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
items.summary: Eval-driven development helps you build AI agents against a consistent set of metrics. Define good behavior, write the eval first, then compare experiments.
items.story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. Our spec looks like this: We’ll evaluate on these guidelines, even though the agent doesn’t have the capability yet. Build a d

items.title: Large Language Models as a Universal Searcher for Open-World Automated Machine Learning
items.summary: Developing effective machine learning models requires complex manual tuning, while current Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) frameworks remain domain-specific and isolate model architecture, training hyperparameter, and data ratio optimization. Here, we bridge this gap by proposing a universal, large language model (LLM)-based AutoML framework that jointly optimizes these configurations for the first time without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. We propose NCode, a unified numerical encoding scheme that translates diverse AutoML design choices into universal discrete sequences and effectively reframes the optimization process as a unified ranking task. Trained solely on optimization trajectories derived from a limited, single-domain vision task, the proposed LLM-based searcher demonstrates impressive cross-task, cross-modality and joint search-space optimization generalizability, achieving state-of-the-art performance across image classification, image segmentation, speaker verification and text-to-image benchmarks. Crucially, it exhibits superior scalability in the large-scale training and joint optimization of a billion-parameter Diffusion Transformer, requiring 896 GPU-days and attaining a state-of-the-art GenEval score of 0.91. By leveraging reinforcement learning to instill Chain-of-Thought reasoning, we provide a systematic way to interpret the LLM-based searcher's internal decision-making mechanisms, revealing its optimization strategy shifted from the early-stage diversity-driven exploration to the late-stage anchor exploitation. Our proposed framework provides a scalable, generalizable, and interpretable pathway toward general-purpose open-world machine learning optimization.

items.title: Correct First, Fast Second: What a Local 7B Code Model Can and Cannot Do for GPU Kernel Optimization
items.summary: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

items.title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

items.title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
items.summary: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

items.content_excerpt: Define semantics once in Unity Catalog and publish them directly to Power BI semantic models Organizations want a single, trusted definition of their business semantics. Revenue, margin, and active customers should mean the same thing in every report, notebook, and AI application. When they don't, business users and AI agents read the same data differently and reach different answers. Finance and sales show different revenue numbers, teams lose trust in their reports, and decisions get made on the wrong numbers. Unity Catalog metric views , part of Unity Catalog semantics, solve this by enabling customers to define business KPIs once in Databricks, in an open, governed semantic layer that sits on top of the lakehouse. At the same time, many of these organizations rely on Power BI as the front end for their business users. Often, organizations have thousands of PowerBI workspaces each with its own Semantic Models, creating a governance and unification nightmare. Furthermore, when each team builds its own metrics and relationships in Power BI, the same logic lives in many places. Reports drift apart, and every definition change means updating each copy. Customers have told us they want both: Databricks as their unified, open semantic layer, and Power BI as their front end. With Publish to Power BI , they can now have both. Every Power BI report uses the same governed UC metric views as AI/BI dashboards and Genie, so teams work from consistent numbers. Business users can build self-serve reports and explore metrics across any dimension without waiting on a data team to model data or write DAX. Data teams maintain one definition in Databricks instead of many copies across systems. Publish on demand from Catalog Explorer, or add a Power BI task to a Lakeflow Job to keep metric views and semantic models in sync in production. With Publish to Power BI or a Power BI task, you can connect Unity Catalog metric views to a Power BI semantic model. Each metric view becomes a table in the model. The metric view’s dimensions (aka Fields) become columns and its measures become DAX measures. Power BI queries the metric view itself (as if it was a table). The metric view stays the source of truth, and joins defined in the metric view run in Databricks. Joined dimensions, such as campaign channel or region, show up in Power BI as ordinary columns, so you don't have to rebuild table relationships in Power BI. items.title: claude-code v2.1.321
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2), now the default Fable model — 1M context, $8/$40 per Mtok with $0.20/Mtok cache reads
  • Added --settings <file> to claude remote-control, which applies a settings file to every session it starts; if the file changes, no new session starts until you restart claude remote-control
  • Fixed MCP OAuth requests sending secrets such as refresh tokens to another host when a server redirected them
  • Fixed a case where a read-only Bash command ran outside the sandbox without a permission prompt
  • Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged a file write from the wrong folder and didn't prompt
  • Fixed deny rules and protected-file prompts not applying to the file that a cp or mv into a directory writes
  • Fixed the "Draws from usage credits" note showing after a switch to Fable on Enterprise seats whose plan includes Fable
  • Fixed the fallback model sometimes declining a request or mentioning a stopped response when the first model was blocked before replying
  • Fixed claude mcp login printing a SEP-2352 issuer warning each time you sign in again to a server that Claude Code registered with
  • Fixed NotebookEdit deleting or overwriting a notebook's first cell when the call named no cell, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed Edit changing the first of several matches, replacing a whole file on an empty old_string, or editing a notebook as text, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed /config showing Manual as the default permission mode when new sessions start in auto mode; pressing Space on "Auto (default)" now saves Don't Ask, not Plan
  • Windows: Fixed FileChanged hooks stopping for paths set through watchPaths after the first shell command, when the session's working directory had a lowercase drive letter
  • Fixed --plugin-dir . and --plugin-dir ./builtin writing generated type files for Claude Code's built-in plugins into a builtin folder
  • Fixed context usage estimates overcounting tool definitions when exact token counts are unavailable
  • Fixed /compact showing twice in Remote Control on web and mobile
  • Fixed plugin auto-updates and /plugin marketplace updates downloading a plugin again for each worktree or folder of a repository
  • Fixed auto mode losing a background subagent's report that had started a turn when the conversation was compacted before Claude answered it
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents staying missing after their folder was removed and came back mid-session, such as with git stash, including after entering a worktree
  • Fixed claude -p sometimes telling Claude that background commands get 30 minutes when they are stopped after 10
  • Fixed pkill, pgrep and pidwait in cloud sessions matching the session's own parent processes
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome and computer use server processes staying alive after their parent exits behind a proxy that stalls connections
  • Fixed a large hook output pointing Claude to a file that held another hook's output from the same tool call
  • Fixed apps that embed Claude Code getting their own PreToolUse hook's ask reason instead of another hook's when both asked
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's ask being lost when another hook's defer finished first and could not be honored
  • Fixed a rare crash on permission prompts and background tasks
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents disappearing from the menu in SDK and desktop sessions after Claude entered a worktree
  • Fixed /desktop on macOS saying Claude Desktop is not installed when it is in ~/Applications
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry repository attributes (vcs.*) missing from Claude Desktop sessions that start on a pre-started process
  • Fixed WebFetch passing "No response from model" to Claude as page content when the model reading the page returned no text; the call now fails with a clear error
  • Fixed screen reader mode delaying the prompt at startup when the system clock moved back while Claude Code was starting
  • Fixed a command's panel sometimes not coming back after a dialog closed, leaving no panel or prompt on screen until the next redraw
  • Fixed a project's MCP server being disconnected after the first message in a Claude Desktop Code tab session when the desktop app has an MCP server or extension of the same name
  • Fixed a turn ending with "API Error: EPROTO: The TLS handshake failed" when the connection broke partway through a reply; the partial reply is kept or the request is retried, as before 2.1.302
  • Fixed high memory use in long sessions that repeatedly read single lines from large files
  • Fixed fast mode losing replies, switching models or retrying for minutes when fast serving is rate-limited, overloaded or failing; it now tries standard speed on the same model first
  • Fixed one request carrying far more background agent reports than intended after Claude was stopped while several were waiting
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop Code tab session to your other sessions staying paused after you typed while Claude was still working
  • Fixed claude agents ignoring --permission-mode, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model, --effort or --agent typed before agents when a flag such as --verbose was also on the line
  • Fixed a case where Remote Control showed as off with "login expired" in the desktop app while its connection was still up, because the app was briefly unable to hand over a sign-in token
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sent with "Queue for later" reaching Claude in the middle of the running turn
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start reading as clean when git status failed; it now reads as unavailable
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start showing the first listed file as staged when its changes were not staged
  • Fixed a hang or out-of-memory crash when a connector in a cloud session lists resources with very long names
  • Fixed Remote Control showing as connected after its connection closed for good while the session's history was still uploading
  • Fixed screen reader mode turning off when you return to a conversation from agent view
  • Fixed screen reader mode y/n questions taking as yes a stray "y" at the end of text typed as the question opened
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that a host is probably not allowed when it is allowed and the network proxy could not connect to it
  • Fixed an MCP server sometimes showing as connected with no tools after it was reconnected or the session's directory changed while its tools were still loading
  • Fixed Bash commands sometimes running in the wrong folder when Claude sent several at once and an earlier one changed folders
  • Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when an upload gets an HTTP 507 from a proxy; the upload now gets a second try
  • Fixed new messages not being saved, and claude -p, SDK and VS Code sessions hanging, when memory ran out while the transcript was being read
  • Fixed sign-in, token refresh and logout waiting indefinitely when something on the network accepts the connection but never answers the TLS handshake
  • Fixed a sent file showing under a different name in the Claude apps when its name hid text-direction or control characters; Claude now refuses to send such a file
  • Fixed sub-agent progress summaries running a request to its end after the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed Bash reads such as grep -r foo "$PWD/src" asking for permission when the same command with the path typed out runs without asking
  • Fixed Claude apps gateway refusing to start when a desktop setting holds a field newer than the gateway, such as a managed MCP server's oauth.omitResource; it now warns and serves it
  • Fixed Bash commands coming back empty for zsh users whose .zshrc sets KSH_OPTION_PRINT
  • macOS: Fixed "Unable to read managed policy settings" at startup when a valid MDM profile was slow to read: the read is retried once, and a timeout is now reported as a timeout
  • Fixed agent view erasing another agent view's saved input text when it restarted for an update with nothing typed
  • Fixed remote sessions giving no reply after a restart when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocked a replayed permission answer; these hooks no longer run on that replay
  • Fixed claude remote-control accepting a y typed without Enter at its first-run question when the terminal's input ended
  • Fixed Claude Desktop not showing spend limit warnings behind a Claude apps gateway whose policy has no code: rules
  • Fixed fullscreen sessions with some plugins ending with an error when a tool result that had got shorter scrolled off the top of the screen
  • Fixed prompt suggestions making extra API requests when the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed PreToolUse mcp_tool hooks on stdio and HTTP MCP servers being skipped when their answer was over 16 MiB; the tool call is now refused
  • Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
  • Fixed claude -p on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
  • Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
  • Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty claude mcp list output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
  • Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
  • Improved the /model picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
  • Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the /device page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
  • Improved claude install and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
  • Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
  • Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
  • Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
  • Improved the agent view's row for a claude --bg --worktree session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
  • Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: /login is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
  • Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
  • Improved claude remote-control's messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
  • Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
  • Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
  • Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
  • Updated the session-feedback message and the allowedProviders setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the forceLoginMethod description to cover every paid Claude plan
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
  • Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
  • Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed allowUnsandboxedCommands: false or allowManagedDomainsOnly, and not to load in dontAsk mode
  • Changed mods' own tool calls ($.tool.call, $.mcp.call) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in dontAsk and -p runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
  • Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to fable: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use /model claude-fable-5-1 to switch back
  • Changed the fast mode labels in /fast, /config and /model to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders inside ~/.claude/plugins no longer load when Claude works on files there
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
  • Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
  • Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of num_hooks and num_success after Bash and PowerShell calls
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
  • Changed AskUserQuestion in claude -p and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented afkTimeoutMs input field
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
  • Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
  • Changed policy_mode: layered in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, match: {} included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
  • Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL variables in the gateway's environment. Set base_url on the upstream to use another endpoint
  • Changed headless sessions to reload mods in .claude/skills when their files change; set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0 to turn this off
  • Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
  • Changed cp and mv spelled by a path, such as /bin/cp, to get the same path checks as cp and mv
  • Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
  • Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
  • Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and names a User-Agent, without asking, so other commands and scheduled runs no longer stop at its prompt
  • Changed Remote Control sessions to keep the folder they were started in: a connected client can no longer move a session to another folder
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces take-overs from an undeclared source: saved data is set aside for cleanupPeriodDays, and options and secrets until claude plugin restore-set-aside
  • [VSCode] Added a warning above the prompt box when both an auth token and an API key are set, matching the terminal's startup warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed a plugin's permission request showing a name with hidden characters: it now reads "a plugin"
